structure: Part 15 of repos/trade-imports-ins-tests: INS transporters, INS accessibility and INS security. Read in full: the 4 transporter specs and their runner under tests/ins/e2e/features/transporters (transporter-type.spec.ts 3 tests, private-transporter.spec.ts 5, commercial-transporter.spec.ts 5, transporter-record.spec.ts 4 — 17 literal test() declarations, not the 21 the partition's covers names; run-transporters.ts declares no test, only the two shared expectations the private and commercial specs both call); the 9 specs under tests/ins/a11y plus its README (address-book-initial-state 2, address-book-filled-state 2, address-book-error-state 3, address-book-list-views 2, address-book-viewports 1 declaration generated twice by a viewport loop, dashboard-views 3, dashboard-viewports 1 generated twice, sign-in 2, a11y-scan-detects-violations 1 test plus 1 test.fail — 21 tests at run time from 19 literal declarations, not the 37 the covers names; several tests scan many pages through test.step, 37 being closer to the number of scans than the number of tests); and the 2 specs under tests/ins/security/address-book (address-book.spec.ts 1 test, address-book-auth.spec.ts 1 test — 2 declarations, not the 6 the covers names). Support code read as context: page-objects/ins/address-book/{transporter-type-page,transporter-form-page,private-transporter-page,commercial-transporter-page,transporter-view-page,list-page,delete-page}.ts, page-objects/ins/index.ts, page-objects/shared/base-page.ts, and (reached from those) shared-form-fields.ts and record-page.ts; domain/ins/constants/{transporter-types,transporter-form,trader-transporter}.ts and (reached from those) address-form.ts and address-book-types.ts; fixtures/{a11y,security,ui}.ts; utils/{a11y-utils,a11y-exclusions,narrow-page-scan}.ts and (reached from a spec) next-page-scan.ts; config/zap.ts; docs/a11y.md and docs/security.md; and the transporter to* methods of flows/ins/journey.ts. Covered: the transporter type question and its two options; the private and commercial transporter forms, their fields, their country rule and what saving stores; the transporter's own page, its rows and its Edit/Delete/Back controls; the Transporter tab's column order and search; every INS page and state scanned for accessibility with its viewport, rule set and exclusion; what the two INS security specs put through the ZAP proxy and how the run is gated; and the gaps — no transporter validation message, no country list, no reference-data lookup, no transporter page scanned for accessibility or driven through ZAP, and no proven transporter edit or delete.

claims.statement: Those radios are excluded because govuk-frontend sets aria-expanded on a conditional-reveal radio input and axe's aria-allowed-attr rule rejects it: an upstream disagreement in component code the service does not own, not a defect in the service.
claims.quote: govuk-frontend's conditional-reveal radios set `aria-expanded` on the radio input in its `radios.mjs`, and axe's `aria-allowed-attr` rule rejects that. This is an upstream disagreement in component code the service does not own, not a defect in the service.

claims.statement: The accessibility documentation's exclusion table names selectors conditionalRadioInput and conditionalReasonRadios, which are not the names the exclusions file exports, so a reader following the table cannot find them.

claims.statement: Security testing is a dynamic scan with OWASP ZAP as a proxy, with Playwright driving real authenticated journeys through it rather than letting ZAP crawl.
claims.quote: A DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) scan using [OWASP ZAP](https://www.zaproxy.org/) as a proxy. Playwright drives real authenticated journeys through it rather than letting ZAP crawl, so it observes what a real session touches and then attacks that.

claims.statement: Security coverage is traffic-driven: a route no spec drives is invisible to the scan, which is why the attacking corpus is curated by hand.
claims.quote: Coverage is therefore **traffic-driven**: a route no spec drives is invisible to the scan. That is why the `@active` corpus is curated by hand rather than generated.

claims.statement: There are two security profiles: a passive one that runs the whole end-to-end suite without attacking, and an attacking one that runs only the curated corpus and is for deliberate use against the local stack.
claims.quote:
| `security`        | The e2e suite, excluding `@active` | No — passive only | Cheap, run broadly              |
| `security:active` | The `@active` suite only           | Yes               | Deliberate; docker-compose only |

claims.statement: The attacking profile is refused on the deployed CDP environments, because the curated corpus deletes records and the attack re-fires each deletion with fuzzed payloads.
claims.quote: **`security:active` is refused on CDP.** The `@active` suite deletes notifications, documents and DLQ messages, and the active scan re-fires each with fuzzed payloads — fine against a disposable stack, destructive against a shared one.

claims.statement: Both INS security specs carry the tag @active, so they run only under the attacking profile and are left out of the passive one.
claims.quote: test.describe('Security scan (ins)', { tag: '@active' }, () => {

claims.statement: A security run fails on any of three conditions: an alert rated as a failure, a scan cut short at its sixty-minute ceiling, or a declared area that no traffic reached.
claims.quote: - **A context with no traffic.** Declared but undriven means its activeScan job scanned nothing and reported clean. Active profile only.

claims.statement: A scan that finishes exactly at the time ceiling is treated as cut short, because an incomplete scan reporting nothing is a false clean.
claims.quote: A scan that finishes at the ceiling was cut short, and an incomplete scan reporting no findings is a false clean.

claims.statement: The proxy listens on a configurable port, 9095 by default, deliberately outside the workspace's two growing port ranges, and its API key is taken from the environment with a local development placeholder.
claims.quote: export const zapPort = process.env.ZAP_PORT || '9095';
claims.note: The default API key in config/zap.ts is a local development placeholder; its value is [REDACTED] here.

claims.statement: The scan treats anything other than an exact request for the attacking profile as passive, so it fails safe.
A per-domain attacking run narrows the no-traffic gate to that domain's own declared areas and the report says the run was scoped; the full run leaves every declared area gated.
claims.quote: Full `security:active` is the authoritative clean bill of health. Per-domain active sets `ZAP_SCOPE` so the no-traffic gate only covers that domain's contexts; the report callout marks the run as scoped.

claims.statement: A run with an unrecognised domain scope is refused outright, naming the domains it accepts.
claims.quote: throw new Error(`Unknown ZAP_SCOPE '${domain}'. Expected one of: ${Object.keys(ZAP_SCOPE_CONTEXTS).join(', ')}`);

claims.statement: The scheduled attacking run is manual only: the nightly schedule stays switched off until an end-to-end run has been verified, and its report is published behind a password because the site it goes to is otherwise public, with reports older than seven days pruned.
claims.quote: The GitHub Action is manual dispatch only; the nightly schedule stays disabled pending a verified end-to-end run.
